opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what's changing. A lot of what we used to call "programming," like translating a clear idea into syntax, looking up APIs, writing boilerplate, and even debugging fairly standard issues, is becoming something models do quite well. If your sense of value comes mainly from typing code fast, that's going to feel threatening, and I don't think it helps to pretend otherwise.

But I'd frame it this way: the bottleneck moves. When writing code becomes cheap, the scarce things are knowing *what* to build, breaking a fuzzy problem into pieces that can actually be verified, and judging whether the output is right. That last one is underrated. Models can generate a lot of code very quickly, and someone has to understand the system well enough to tell when something is subtly wrong, or when it passes tests but isn't what you meant. So I'd actually say fundamentals matter more, not less. You need a good mental model of how systems work, even if you're not writing every line yourself.

The second thing is practical: just use the tools seriously, every day. Not as a toy, and not only for autocomplete. Try handing over bigger chunks of work, see where it breaks, and develop intuition for what to delegate and what to keep. People who do this build a kind of muscle, almost like learning to manage a team, and that gap compounds quickly. The people who struggle most are often the ones who tried it once a year ago, decided it wasn't good, and haven't updated since.

And maybe the third point is mindset. I think the role is shifting from "person who writes code" toward "person who owns outcomes," someone closer to a product thinker, an architect, or a researcher, who uses code as one of many levers. That's a bigger job in some sense. It's uncomfortable because the ground keeps moving, but I'd rather see it as leverage: one person can now build things that used to need a whole team. The question is whether you position yourself to use that leverage, or wait for it to happen to you.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest about what's actually changing. For a long time, the bottleneck in programming was writing code. You had an idea, and then you spent most of your time translating that idea into syntax that a machine would accept. That part is basically going away. A model can now write a few hundred lines, run them, see the error, fix it, and iterate much faster than any of us can type.

So the question becomes: what's left? And I think a lot is left, it's just different.

The first thing is problem definition. Models are very good at solving a well-specified problem. They're much worse at figuring out which problem is worth solving, or noticing that the problem you asked for is actually the wrong problem. A good engineer who can look at a messy situation and say "the real issue is here, and the right abstraction is this" is more valuable now, not less, because the cost of executing on a good idea has collapsed.

The second thing is taste. When code is cheap, you get a lot of it, and someone has to decide what's good. Is this architecture going to hold up in six months? Is this interface going to confuse the next person? Those judgments come from experience, and I don't think you can get them without having written a lot of code yourself. So I'd actually tell younger people: don't skip the fundamentals. Understand how things work underneath. Not because you'll hand-write everything, but because you need to be able to evaluate what the model produces and know when it's wrong.

The third thing is working with the agent, and this is something I think about a lot from the research side. Programming is becoming more like managing. You specify, you delegate, you check the result, you give feedback. The skill is in writing a good spec, setting up a good environment where the agent can verify its own work, and designing the feedback loop. Tests, evals, clear interfaces. People who are good at building that scaffolding will get much more out of these tools than people who just prompt and hope.

And honestly, I'd encourage programmers to think bigger. If one person plus an agent can do what a small team used to do, then the ambition of what you try to build should go up. The people who adapt best, I think, are not the ones defending the old job, but the ones who realize the leverage just went up ten times and ask what they can do with it.

astra-6.text:
I think programmers should focus less on how much code they write and more on whether they can solve the right problem. If AI makes implementation cheaper, then deciding what to build, explaining the requirements clearly, and checking whether the result actually works become more important.

That doesn’t mean you no longer need to understand programming. You need enough understanding to judge the AI’s output, debug failures, and recognize when a solution is unnecessarily complicated. It’s easy to generate something that looks plausible; it’s harder to know whether it’s correct and maintainable.

So my advice would be to use AI on real projects and gradually explore how much responsibility you can give it. Pay attention to where it succeeds and where you still need to intervene. The valuable skill is being able to turn an ambiguous goal into a working system, using whatever tools are available.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to stop defining yourself by the act of writing code. Code is a way to solve problems, and AI is changing how much of that process we can automate. But someone still needs to decide what problem matters, what a good solution looks like, and whether the result actually works.

For programmers, I’d suggest two things. First, use AI seriously in your daily work. Try delegating a whole task, see where it fails, and learn how to give it context and verify its output. You develop judgment through that experience.

Second, keep building your fundamentals. When generating code becomes cheap, understanding and evaluating code becomes more valuable. You need enough knowledge to recognize a flawed design, debug an unexpected interaction, or question an answer that looks convincing.

I also think programmers can become more ambitious. Something that previously required a team might become feasible for one person. So instead of only asking, ‘How can I do my current job faster?’ ask, ‘What can I build now that I couldn’t build before?’
